summary: Pseudowires are a common tunneling mechanism and can compete for resources with other pseudowires and with traffic such as TCP flows. This informational RFC discusses when that competition is acceptable, so PW traffic does not harm others or add more to congestion than it should.

eli5.summary: Tunnels carrying traffic should share the road fairly and slow down when it is jammed. This sets out when they must.

questions: what is a circuit breaker for pseudowires
subtitle: How network tunnels can coexist fairly with other traffic

tldr.problem: Pseudowires are tunnels that carry encapsulated traffic over packet networks, but they may compete for bandwidth with other traffic like TCP flows without any built-in congestion control.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes two cases: elastic pseudowires carrying TCP-like traffic respond to congestion automatically, and inelastic TDM pseudowires consume fixed bandwidth but degrade in service before becoming harmful, so shutting them down when service fails prevents congestion damage.
tldr.outcome: Pseudowires do not require special congestion-avoidance mechanisms; elastic PWs behave safely, and inelastic PWs are acceptable if they terminate when they can no longer deliver acceptable service.

facts.label: Maximum acceptable packet loss for TDM

today: RFC 7893 is an Informational RFC published in June 2016. It has not been obsoleted or superseded. The document provides guidance for deploying pseudowires in unmanaged network environments where they must coexist with other traffic types, and the framework it presents remains applicable to modern network designs.

sections.title: Pseudowires and Shared Networks
sections.content: A pseudowire (PW) is a tunnel that encapsulates one type of traffic (such as Ethernet or TDM) inside another network, such as IPv4 or IPv6, allowing service providers to transport native services transparently across packet networks. When multiple PWs share network capacity with other traffic—including regular TCP flows and other pseudowires—there is no inherent mechanism to allocate bandwidth or prevent one PW from harming neighbors. The RFC examines when this competition is acceptable and when special safeguards are needed.
sections.eli5: Tunnels carry traffic through shared pipes. When many pipes compete for the same space, you need rules about who backs off when things get tight.

sections.title: Two Types of Pseudowires
sections.content: Pseudowires fall into two categories based on how they respond to congestion. Elastic pseudowires carry TCP-like traffic that slows down when the network is congested, reducing its bandwidth consumption. Inelastic pseudowires, such as those carrying Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) voice or circuit data, require a fixed amount of bandwidth and cannot reduce it when congestion occurs. The analysis shows that elastic and inelastic PWs require different considerations but neither needs special congestion control if operated correctly.
sections.eli5: Some tunnels are like streaming video—they slow down when the network is busy. Others are like phone calls—they need the same bandwidth always, or they fail completely.

sections.title: Elastic Pseudowires and TCP Fairness
sections.content: An elastic pseudowire carrying TCP flows behaves the same way as the same flows sent directly without encapsulation. If a router drops a packet due to congestion, the individual TCP sender inside the tunnel responds by retransmitting and backing off, just as it would outside the tunnel. Therefore, elastic PWs do not gain or lose an unfair advantage by being tunneled; they receive the same drop probability as non-encapsulated traffic and respond identically. An aggregated elastic PW containing multiple TCP flows reduces its total bandwidth consumption by the same percentage as the individual flows back off, making the PW as TCP-friendly as its constituent flows.
sections.eli5: If you pack several TCP conversations into a tunnel, the tunnel slows down the same amount as those conversations would if sent separately.

sections.title: Inelastic TDM Pseudowires and TCP Comparison
sections.content: Inelastic TDM PWs are constant-bit-rate services (such as T1 at 1.544 Mbps or E1 at 2.048 Mbps) that cannot adapt to congestion. The RFC uses the TCP Friendly Rate Control (TFRC) formula to compare TDM PW bandwidth consumption to that of a TCP flow under identical network conditions. The analysis shows that a TDM PW is acceptable if it consumes no more bandwidth than a comparable TCP flow, expressed as the condition D < 4S / (BW * f(p)), where D is one-way delay, S is segment size, BW is the TDM bandwidth, and f(p) is a function of packet loss probability. For most realistic parameters—especially when TDM packets are sized for low latency (256 or 1024 bytes)—TDM PWs satisfy this condition across a range of network conditions.
sections.eli5: Using math, the RFC shows that a TDM tunnel running at a fixed speed is usually less greedy than a single TCP flow fighting for the same pipe.

sections.title: Service Degradation and Circuit Breakers
sections.content: TDM service quality degrades with packet loss before a TDM PW becomes harmful. ITU-T G.826 standards limit errors per second; TDM services typically degrade or become unusable when packet loss exceeds 0.5% to 2%, depending on the encapsulation method. This degradation naturally occurs before the TDM PW consumes TCP-unfriendly amounts of bandwidth. Therefore, if a TDM PW automatically shuts down when it can no longer deliver acceptable service (following G.826 criteria), it will never inflict more harm than a single TCP flow. For systems that do not automatically shut down failing TDM service, a transport circuit breaker may be deployed as a last resort to terminate a TDM PW that persistently fails quality thresholds.
sections.eli5: When a phone call gets too choppy to hear, it fails. By then, the tunnel is using less bandwidth than a normal TCP conversation would.
